en: *Kṣitigarbha’s Daśatattvasaṃgraha* according to the tradition of Jñānapāda [in the retinue of Vanaratna; died at mChims phu], IASWR MBB-II-208 (missing folia: 2)
[1r] [Cover Page] [1v] Homage to the Buddha!
Having bowed to Vajrasattva and the assembly of his spiritual sons,
the ten principles are now explained according to the sequence of the Jñānapāda tradition.

The protection wheel, the wheel, recitation, the two consecrations, *haṭha*, the offering (*bali*), the counter-attack (*pratyaṅgira*), the opening of the seal (*puṭodghāṭa*), and the principles (*tattvas*); these are the ten [topics] in successive order.
Having created the world through the arrays of light rays arising from one's own seed-syllable placed at the heart,
and having mentally drawn forth the Buddhas and others by means of those very rays in front [of oneself],...
Having performed prostration, as well as worship, confession, and rejoicing,
and having gone for refuge to the Buddha and the others, one then relies upon the path.
Then, having generated the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), one should recollect the three gateways to liberation;
indeed, in the corners [of the mandala], one should place Ṭakki, Daṇḍa, Bala, and Acala.
Uṣṇīṣacakravartin is above, while Sumbharāja is traditionally held to be below.
All the wrathful deities are born from the syllable HŪṂ; Uṣṇīṣa is supreme, being born from BHRŪṂ.
All stand in the pratyālīḍha posture upon the sun-disk in the sky, their bodies embraced by their innate consorts who are joined with the savoring of bliss.
Other than Prajñāpadmāntaka and Uṣṇīṣa, the others are proclaimed to be blue;
Prajñāntaka and the rest are white, red, and yellow, respectively.
Excluding Yamāntaka and Padmāntaka, those others have Akṣobhya as their crown ornament;
for Yamāri, Śāśvata is on the crown, while for the other, it is Amitābha.
A mallet, a goad, a staff, a blue staff,
a lotus, a trident, a thunderbolt, a sword, a yellow wheel, and a vajra.
The mark of truth is on the right hand of the one-eyed Acala;
on the left are a discus and a noose, and he is adorned with ornaments of serpents.
Covered by the staff-like arms of his wrath, with a radiance filled with garlands of flames,
it whirled in a clockwise direction with great speed, appearing as if motionless.
Those wrathful deities who abide on the ten spokes, possessing great strength and prowess,
should be meditated upon as motionless, having the nature of bliss consisting of wisdom and means.
Ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, the knowledge and vision of liberation,
and liberation itself— these five aggregates are supramundane.
Those Krodhas, purified by the ten knowledges and characterized by the mirror-like sameness, discernment, and purity of vigor, should be meditated upon with complete certainty.
For the sake of protecting the one who has mounted the wheel from falling into the Lesser Vehicle,
the vajra and the syllable *hūṃ* reside within the hollow of the hub, having entered the heart.
The mudrā is the source of phenomena (dharmodayā); within it, one should visualize the celestial palace and so forth. || o ||
There, from the syllable *bhrūṃ*, there arises the eternal [deity] together with his consort, born from the wheel;
he emits streams of Buddhas that pervade the sky, and is endowed with the square [mandala] and other features.

One should visualize a peaked pavilion, its interior divided into distinct sections of pure red, serving as the divine seat upon which a universal lotus is positioned, itself occupied by the moon and the sun.
There, upon the central seat, is the Moon endowed with the thirty-two major marks;
there, amidst the [eighty] secondary characteristics, is the syllable HŪṂ produced from the sound HŪṂ.
From that process of expansion and withdrawal, there arises Vajrasattva,
whose body is like crystal and the moon, with a blue face at the front, a red right face, and a white other [left] face.
In his right hand he holds a vajra-sword, and in his left, an excellent jewel-lotus;
he is the embodiment of wisdom and skillful means, the glorious refuge for the prosperity of the world.
One should meditate on oneself as Samantabhadra, radiating shimmering light;
here, all the deities, beginning with the Wrathful Ones, have three faces and six arms.
Their own voices are wonderful with the non-dual bliss obtained from the union with the limbs of their respective consorts;
all hold a sword in the right hand, and a jewel and a lotus in the left.
Those who have a lotus in the right hand have a jewel, while for those who have a wheel, it is on the left.
For all of them, the right face is blue, and the face of the Blue One is white.
The left [hand] of all is white, while that of the White and Black [deities] is red;
this is because he has observed the world, a vessel to be disciplined through great passion.
With the sound of the mantra, one should cause the assembly of Jinas to enter within oneself;
and [one should visualize] the forms of Locanā, Rūpavajrā, and the others as the passion for Wisdom.
Having projected the goddesses in nine ways, one should cause them to enter into their respective vidyās;
then, [one should visualize] the maṇḍala arising from sexual union, situated within the lotus of one's own consort.
Having emanated the entire world here, he should cause it to enter for the sake of consolation,
together with all the Buddhas who pervade space and arise from the internal melting of the vajra.
One should sprinkle [the world] for the sake of non-retrogression and for the attainment of the fruit of the knowledge of reality;
seeing that world comforted, one should emit it by means of its respective seeds.
From these seed-syllables— kṣiṃ, jraṃ, khaṃ, gaṃ, skaṃ, and m— itself,
one should [visualize] the six deities beginning with Kṣitigarbha in their respective order, through the purification of the eyes and other sense faculties.
From the seed-syllables *hūṃ*, *vaṃ*, *hoḥ*, *khaṃ*, and *raṃ*, [one arises] in the form of Rūpavajrā and the others;
and by means of these—*lāṃ*, *māṃ*, *pāṃ*, and *tāṃ*—[one arises] with the intrinsic nature of Locanā and the others.
From the seed-syllables *vuṃ*, *āṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *khaṃ*, and *hūṃ*, the Buddhas, whose forms consist of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, [emerge];
with *oṃ*, *āṃ*, and *hūṃ*, the mind is interlaced with the radiant *ho* syllables from above and below.
That [semen] flows clearly from within the interior of the secret lotus due to passion;
through that great passion, both wisdom and means become liquefied.
By means of the verses beginning with "O Vajra," the assembly of goddesses and those belonging to their families [are established];
and the Bodhisattvas everywhere are fashioned in the form of Vajrasattva by the skillful one.
By means of the limb of gentle cultivation, which is conjoined with the fruit of maturation,
one should generate the wisdom of equality and thereby turn back the afflicted mind.
The fulfillment of the world's purpose proceeds through the enjoyment and emanation bodies of the Dharma;
therefore, one should produce the limbs of the practice, such as the empowerment of the secret of the mind and so forth.
In the moons at one's own heart, throat, and head, [one visualizes] the true lords HŪṂ ĀḤ OṂ and JĀḤ,
residing in the centers of vajras, lotuses, and wheels, with seed-syllables situated within their respective heart-marks.

Having meditated on that, one should worship the Lords situated in the directions through the forms of Rūpavajrā and the others, which arise from the rays of those seed-syllables, for those who possess the three vajras.
In this common maṇḍala, one should meditate upon the Leader according to one's wish:
he who is born from the attachment to existence, who is infinite, whose attachment is equanimous, and who partakes in the cessation of suffering.
Having performed the sprinkling with illusion, one becomes of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
"Oṃ, I am of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
Through the arising of the fruit that flows from the limbs of gentle service (*mṛdu-sevā*), [the obstacle] is removed.
The contaminated storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is the source from which the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna) arises.
Having filled the eyes and other sense organs with the seed-syllables Kṣitīśa, Kuliśa, Ākāśa, Lokeśa, Svastika, and Bhadra, one shall attain omniscience.
One should meditate on the appearance of the essential nature of the eternal [deity] and so forth, bearing its characteristic marks;
rising up in accordance with that [meditation], one should perceive the fluid [nature of reality] like a bird in flight.
Through the realization of the reality that is like an illusion, from the melting of that [reality], there arises from the seed-syllable Maṃ;
from the sword produced by that seed-syllable Maṃ, one should oneself become Mañjuvajra.
His face has the appearance of saffron, and he is blue on the left and white on the other;
adorned with the ornaments of a youth, he is uniquely beautiful through the bliss of wisdom.
Embraced by his excellent Prajñā with two arms, holding his own Prajñā,
he has hands bearing a radiant sword and an excellent arrow, and a blue lotus and a bow.
One should meditate on Akṣobhya as black, produced from a vajra born from the syllable *hūṃ* in the center, having been accomplished by the emanations of the surging flood of Buddhas.
One should request that empowerment through the verses beginning with *cittavajra*.
Having caused the requested *cittavajra* and so forth to enter into one’s own mind and so on, if—
One should possess that sense of identity by means of the mantra beginning with "Oṃ Sarva...
because human effort is possible within that gentle preliminary stage of practice.
Conceptual constructions and mental elaborations are exhausted through the moment of arising in discernment;
above the mind-vajra, the wisdom-being (jñānasattva) is considered to be the pledge-being (samayasattva).
Born from the sign of his own seed-syllable upon the moon, with his heart marked by the sign of his own seed-syllable,
he impels the Lords situated in the directions by means of the light-rays from the heart of the Knowledge Being (jñānasattva).
Consecrated by the vidyās arising from that light and by the nectar-water from the filled jars,
the glorious Lord, the Kuleśa, becomes the Crown.
In that which arises from the Great Accomplishment (mahāsādhana) and is named the Purity of the Fruit,
the active consciousness (pravṛttivijñāna) has ceased due to the occurrence of the performance of duties.
One should purify one's own innate wisdom through the [five stages] beginning with the outflow (niṣyanda) and the intermediate ones;
and within this [wisdom], one should dissolve the atoms sequentially at the head, heart, navel, secret place, and the ends of the feet.
Having filled the heart of the lotus with the five Buddhas by means of the seed-syllables Oṃ Hūṃ Svā Āḥ Hā, which consist of the families beginning with Śāśvata, [one should recite] Hūṃ Āḥ.
Having thoroughly purified the Buddhas with that [mantra], one should cause them to be impassioned with *HŪṂ* and the True Vajra:
*OṂ SARVATATHĀGATĀNURĀGAṆAVAJRASVABHĀVĀTMAKO ’HAṂ*.

Having established within oneself the circle of Buddhas pervading the sky— marked by the moon in the heart and possessing the radiance of the heart— one should visualize it as the form of the True Thought (saccinta), resting upon a vajra-lotus.
Having generated the host of Jinas there by means of their respective seed-syllables and stabilized them,
one should emit them according to this procedure for the purification of one's own knowledge of the world.
Having exhorted the Lord Akṣobhya, the Victor who accomplishes the purpose of great hatred,
[he addressed] the Vajra-holder, the Lord of Vajras, who has the luster of a sapphire.
Having withdrawn [the deities] into himself, the illustrious one should establish them within his own being through all their aspects;
he should contemplate the first [deity], Jinajik, the Conqueror who effects the purpose of great delusion.

Having abandoned the Lord who bears the discus, one should meditate upon Ratneśa— known as "Ratnadhṛk"— who is yellow in color and holds a jewel aloft with both hands, within the orb of the full moon.
Having cast [the seed] toward the southern direction, one should visualize the face of the Youth;
[thus arises] ĀROLIṄ, the Lord of Speech, the Sovereign who accomplishes the purpose of Great Passion.
One should visualize the red Amogheśa, holding a lotus on his back, seated upon a solar throne;
he is the holder of wisdom and bestows the purpose of generating great envy.
One should meditate on the one who wields the sword, greenish-dark in hue, from the northern sun;
all [the deities] wear matted hair and crowns, and are adorned with all ornaments.
But when the leader [of the mandala] is Śāśvatādi,
the skillful practitioner should withdraw that form from the mandala into himself by means of that leader, as previously described.
Furthermore, one should meditate on Akṣobhya as the leader in each respective place;
and in the southeast, there is Moharati, while Locanā is the mistress of the body.
Dveṣarati, Citteśa, and Candramāmakī are in the southwest; Rāgarati, Vāgīśā, and Pāṇḍaravāsini are in the northwest.
And in the northeast is Vajrarati; Tārā is remembered as being like Ratneśa.
[She holds] a divine red lotus, a wheel, and a yellow water-lily.

The signs for these [deities] have been taught in sequence; the remaining ones should be assigned according to their respective lords, in the four corners starting from the southeast, and on both sides of the eastern door.
The appearances of the body and so forth are known as Rūpavajrā and the others by virtue of the three principles;
likewise, there are the mirror, the lute, the scent-conch, and the vessel of taste.
Their garments, *dharmodayās*, and emblems are prescribed in sequence;
they are seated upon moons, wear jeweled crowns, and are in union with their respective consorts as skillful means.
The goddesses are endowed with all ornaments and the erotic sentiment, and are non-dual in compassion.
At the eastern gate is Krodhaparyaṅka, radiant with the form of Citteśa;
he is Yamāntakṛt, the destroyer of diseases and the annihilator of the objects of cognition and the sentient beings.
In the eastern direction, he is Kāyeśa, terrible with fierce eyes; at the western gate, he is Aparārjita.

He is Prajñāntakṛt, the destroyer of desire, who abandons the afflictions through the vision of the self. At the rear gate, he is Aśvakandhara, the destroyer of the mass of the evils of birth and death.
Padmāntakṛt is the destroyer of false views; he is proclaimed as Vāgīśa and Abhoga.
Akṣobhya, Abhoga, and Vighnaghna are in the north, while Amṛtakuṇḍalin is at the gate as Vighnāntakṛt, due to the purification of the deities of action and the like.
With furrowed brows, their hair, eyebrows, beards, and eyes blazing upward,
with averted faces and lolling tongues, they laugh fiercely with bared fangs;
all these wrathful deities possess solar mandalas and shine with the brilliance of the sun.
These [deities] should be meditated upon as holding a vajra, a mallet, a staff, a lotus, their own vajra, and so forth in their hands;
their bodies are adorned with fierce serpents, they are embraced by their respective consorts (vidyā),
they have short and pendulous bellies, and they gaze at the three mandalas with non-dual vision.
Having beheld the perfected maṇḍala through the state of the mass of bliss,
one should summon the Buddhas of the wisdom-maṇḍala with the goads of the seed-syllables at the heart;
then, having offered water for the guest-offering (*argha*) and so forth, which has been consecrated by mantras and is endowed with sandalwood, flowers, and other offerings.

Having placed that wheel upon the wheel, one should meditate upon it as being empowered by the eyes, body, and so forth, and as being sprinkled as before; [one should contemplate] the outflow and so forth up to the highest degree. On the crowns of the Buddhas is the Vajra-holder (Vajradhara), while the others are sprinkled by their own lords.
Having sealed the cause with the fruit and the fruit with the cause,
the gatekeepers are considered to be the Lords of Body, Speech, and Mind— Akṣobhya, Vāgīśa,
and Cittaiśa. Thus, having sprinkled [the deity] with the light from one's own heart, [one visualizes him] seated within the lotus of wisdom.

Having worshipped the city [of the body] beginning with form, which arises from the pores of the skin, by means of the Form-Vajra and others, one should worship oneself and the Lords of Sages; thus becoming the essence of both the worship and the object of worship, one recites: *Oṃ, I am of the nature of the Vajra-worship of all Tathāgatas*.
One should praise the wheel according to its own nature with the verses beginning "Akṣobhya.
One should meditate on the vajra, arisen from the syllable *HŪṂ*, situated in the intermediate space;
below that, one should visualize the lotus, arisen from the syllable *ĀḤ*.
One should place those marked with the syllable Oṃ and filled with nectar in the center there. Now, the consecrations are explained.

The two *sekas*—namely, the secret (*guhya*) and the wisdom (*prajñā*)—are specified because they are primary; these two alone are presented as the nature of reality (*tattva*), since the others are subordinate to them and are external by way of purifying the body.
(iv. Secret Initiation)

Therein, the mantra-practitioner—who has received the initiation of the Vidyā-ācārya, is endowed with faith, and has properly propitiated the true Guru—having prepared a [consort] who possesses the heard commitments (*samaya*) and so forth, who is in the prime of youth, and who is adorned with all ornaments according to the twelvefold classification and other divisions; having placed her to the left of the Guru and worshipped the Guru together with his Prajñā through various offerings; and having performed the mandala-circle and other rites, the practitioner, in a secluded place adorned with various offerings, upon a mandala drawn with colored powders or upon a cloth mandala, in one part thereof:
Seated upon a bed such as a couch that is pleasing to the mind, one should entreat the Guru with secret verses for the sake of the secret initiation:
"By the grace of your feet, I have attained the unsurpassed practice.
Now, O Lord, grant your favor by means of the jewel of initiation."
O Lord, just as the illustrious Mahāsukhanātha revealed to the Buddhas, the Protectors, that which is called the pure reality, so too, O Lord, be gracious to me.
O Lord, lift me up from this abode of all sufferings;
show compassion to me, who am without a protector, and cut through all my sorrows.
"O Lord, apart from your lotus feet, I have no other refuge;
therefore, be gracious, O foremost of Buddhas, hero of the world, great bliss!
Having heard this supreme and divine rite of supplication, thus:
Having generated compassion for his disciple, the illustrious Guru, an ocean of virtues, [acted].
Having become serene of face, compassionate, and joyful,
he should cause them to hear the divine vow, the supreme and special secret.
"O son, you would have to kill living beings, speak untruthful words,
take what is not given, and consort with the wives of others."
O noble one, you must maintain this supreme vow of the covenant:
excrement, urine, flesh, blood, and fifthly, that which arises from the mind.
And the lamp of cows, horses, and so forth, must be consumed by you daily according to the ritual procedures for purification; this is a most wonderful commitment.

Then the preceptor, situated in the center of the entire circle of deities, having cast the five nectars and so forth into the lotus of his own vidyā, and having properly empowered the Wisdom Goddess— who is identical with him and joined in yoga— through the non-dual yoga of wisdom and means, he emits various rays of light from the heart of his own Jñānasattva.

Having established all sentient beings in the coemergent great bliss (*sahajamahāsukha*), one should, by means of that very sound of union, summon all the Tathāgatas and cause them to enter through the mouth; having melted them with the passion of supreme great bliss, one should perceive them according to their respective locations through the distinctions of joy (*ānanda*) and so forth, and stabilize them. Having sustained the coemergent state for as long as possible by means of the *phaṭ* syllable, the wind, and so on, and having visualized the disciple in the form of Vairocana—or as one's own chosen deity (*iṣṭayogin*)—one should empower the eyes, body, and other parts.

That [substance], having fallen by way of the vajra-path into the lotus of one's own consort—whether it has reached there or not—one should cause it to fall into the mouth of the disciple by means of the two, namely Ānāma and Jyeṣṭhā. Some say it is by means of the vajra itself being pressed by those two.

Then the disciple, possessing the yoga of the deity, saying "O, what bliss!", should partake of it with the conviction: "This is the supreme nectar that dispels the darkness of all ignorance. Some say it should be given by the Prajñā in the same manner.
This is the excellent state of consecration for all Vajras.
All vajras and the extensive arrays of supreme activities are accomplished.
Thus concludes the secret empowerment.

(v. Prajñājñānābhiṣeka) Then, having taken up that which arises from the mind— situated upon a lotus and accompanied by flowers— one should offer it with one's own mouth into the mouth of the Vidyā for the sake of worship, [the offering] proceeding via the vajra.
Having thus caused the disciple to grasp [the teachings], the Guru then makes a formal request to him.
Then, having first empowered that maiden as before, the Guru,
holding her hands above and below, should transmit the Vidyā into her.
This delightful dhāraṇī of yours has been devised by the Buddhas for practice;
through the application of the sequence of the wheel, experience true bliss.
Through contact with wisdom, the illustrious one should clearly perceive reality, while observing the mind within the jewel from the vajra-paryaṅka posture. Thus it is said.
She too, being worthy, should then proclaim the vow to him:
"O Vajradhara, are you able to consume feces, urine, and so forth?"
Blood, semen, and likewise flesh, as well as supreme devotion toward women, and the kissing of the lotus of the womb— O Wielder of the Thunderbolt, tell me of the great bliss [arising from these].
Then the Blessed One, the wielder of the vajra, smiling, said this:
"O Goddess, why would I not be able to consume semen, blood, and so forth?
Women must always be honored with kisses and the very act of sexual union."
With her excellent limbs uncovered, she should show her own lotus in its true nature, saying:
"Oh, my lotus is endowed with all happiness;
I stand before him who serves it according to the prescribed rite."
This realm of phenomena is pure, liberating the realm of sentient beings;
it is the King of Great Bliss himself, established within all existents.
In the center of the bhaga is the space adorned by the five voids;
it is endowed with a pericarp and filaments and embellished by eight petals.
Situated there, it constantly flows as nectar in the form of a drop.
He commands him: "Enjoy liberation! Hoḥ!"
Then, having correctly discerned that channel of Vajradhātvīśvarī through the words of the guru and by means of non-dual union with wisdom (*prajñā*),
he should slightly stimulate it with his finger and further with a tongue-spoon.
That channel, the supreme carrier of sexual bliss,
attains expansion when the Lord of the Dhātus has entered the practitioner who possesses the wheel of his chosen deity.
Seated upon a comfortable seat, the Guru, concealed by a cloth or similar screen,
beholds the son— illuminated by the rays of light from his heart and impelled by the seed-syllable and its radiance— by means of the Buddhas.
Having sprinkled [the disciple] with excellent jars filled with the water of gnosis, with the nectar-water of the vajra-lotus,
and by means of Rūpavajrā and the others, one should cause him to enter therein.

Then the disciple, having expanded [the visualization] toward sentient beings as much as desired according to the teacher’s instruction, should focus on the *bodhicitta*, release it, and himself take it up with his tongue while it rests upon the lotus and drink it. According to some, the Wisdom Consort herself should place it from her mouth into his mouth. Then, requested by them with appropriate worship and fees, the teacher, while they both remain in the squatting posture (*utkuṭuka*) as before, should place his two hands upon their hands (held in the left) and his right hand upon their heads, and bestow the Vidyā-vow:
"From this day forward, this maiden has been properly given by me to this practitioner."
May the Tathāgatas recognize this for the sake of attaining great enlightenment.
This delightful dhāraṇī of yours was devised by the Buddhas as that which is to be cultivated;
through no other means can there be Buddhahood, nor is this triple world pure [otherwise].
All phenomena are non-dual, yet they are characterized by a state of duality;
therefore, you should not effect a separation from this [duality] within saṃsāra.
This is that unsurpassed vidyā-vow of all the Buddhas;
the fool who transgresses it shall not attain supreme accomplishment.
Thus one should bestow the vow of knowledge; so it is said.
[On 28r] [Ends on 41r] Thus ends the procedure for opening the casket (saṃpuṭodghāṭavidhi). || o ||
By the merit I have acquired through withdrawing the ten principles (tattvas),
may that person who has fully realized those ten principles become perfectly established.
This *Daśatattvasaṃgraha* is the work of the scholar Kṣitigarbha. || 0 ||
